summary: At a Sabbath meal in a leading Pharisee's house, Jesus heals a swollen man while watched closely, then exposes status competition through seats at table. He tells the host to invite people who cannot repay — poor, disabled, and excluded guests whose resurrection reward interrupts patronage exchange. A great-banquet story answers a pious remark by showing invited people making plausible excuses while the house fills from streets and roads. Turning to large traveling crowds, Jesus demands allegiance above family and life, cross-bearing, sober cost-counting, and renunciation of possessions. Tower builder, outmatched king, and salt make clear that enthusiasm without durable commitment is not discipleship.
whyItMatters: Luke puts hospitality, honor, repayment, and discipleship under one critique. God's feast overturns social reciprocity, but accepting the invitation is not cheap sentiment: followers must relinquish the family, status, and property claims that compete with the road to Jerusalem.

context.author: The anonymous author, traditionally identified as Luke, setting meal teaching and cost sayings inside the Jerusalem journey
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider Greek-reading audience; the chapter addresses patronage, status, family loyalty, and property
context.date: Commonly dated around AD 80–90, after AD 70; earlier dates in the 60s and later ones into the early second century are defended; part of the travel narrative
context.setting: A leading Pharisee's Sabbath table, imagined banquet and streets, then the road with large crowds
context.literaryForm: Healing controversy, banquet etiquette wisdom, invitation parable, hyperbolic call sayings, and planning comparisons

outline.heading: Sabbath meal, watched healing, and silenced experts
outline.note: Watched at a ruler's house, he asks if healing on the Sabbath is lawful; they are silent, and he heals a man with dropsy

outline.heading: Lowest seat and honor received rather than seized
outline.note: Seeing guests choose the best seats, he tells them to take the lowest place, so the host may say 'Friend, move up higher'.

outline.heading: Invite those unable to repay
outline.note: He tells his host to ask the poor, lame and blind, not friends or rich neighbors; the host will be repaid in the resurrection

outline.heading: Great banquet, excuses, streets, and roads
outline.note: Invited guests make excuses: a field, oxen, a wife; the angry master has the poor and lame brought in, then others from the highways

outline.heading: Family, self, cross, and the cost of following
outline.note: Turning to the crowds, he says whoever doesn't disregard family and his own life, or bear his own cross, 'can't be my disciple'.

outline.heading: Tower, king, renunciation, and salt
outline.note: A man counts the cost before building a tower, a king weighs ten thousand against twenty thousand; flat salt is thrown out

keyVerses.text: For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”
keyVerses.why: Luke's reversal moves from table etiquette toward God's judgment of status.

keyVerses.text: “The lord said to the servant, ‘Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
keyVerses.why: On one common reading, the command answers the hesitation of socially excluded guests; its later coercive use contradicts the host's generous feast.

keyVerses.text: So therefore, whoever of you who doesn’t renounce all that he has, he can’t be my disciple.
keyVerses.why: Luke refuses to let discipleship leave control of possessions untouched.

questions.question: What condition does the man at the meal have?
questions.answer: The Greek hydropikos refers to dropsy or edema, visible swelling from fluid retention which can come from heart, kidney or liver problems. Luke uses the body before them to ask whether Sabbath and legal expertise serve life. Modern readers should not turn the diagnosis into a moral symbol the text does not state.

questions.question: Is Jesus teaching a strategy for getting promoted at dinner?
questions.answer: He begins with realistic honor etiquette but ends with the general reversal of self-exaltation and humility. Taking the lowest place merely to manipulate a public upgrade would reproduce the competition. The next instruction — invite those who cannot repay — dismantles the status economy more deeply.

questions.question: Why specifically invite poor and disabled people?
questions.answer: Jesus notes that friends and rich neighbors invited to dinner ‘might also return the favor, and pay you back’ (14:12). Jesus directs hospitality toward people structurally unable to repay in that economy. Disability is not a symbol for sin here; named people are welcomed as guests, and the host must release control of social return.

questions.question: Are the banquet excuses obviously dishonest?
questions.answer: Land inspection, testing oxen, and new marriage are plausible obligations, which is the point: ordinary goods can become refusals when the invitation arrives. The story does not condemn farms, work, or marriage universally; it reveals priorities and the danger of assuming one's reserved place can be accepted later.

questions.question: Does ‘compel them to come in’ authorize forced conversion?
questions.answer: Most readers today say no. On one common reading, people from roads and hedges might not believe a prestigious invitation truly included them, and urgent persuasion overcomes hesitation so the house fills. Augustine used the phrase to argue for compelling the Donatists into the church (Augustine, Letter 185.24), but on the common reading force violates the parable's gift and Jesus's refusal of retaliatory violence.

questions.question: Does Jesus literally command hatred of family?
questions.answer: The Greek word, ‘hate’ (the WEB has ‘disregard’), carries a Semitic contrast of lesser allegiance, stated in maximally shocking form, and Luke includes one's own life. The demand is real: kinship cannot overrule Jesus's road. Yet this Gospel commands love of enemies and care for the vulnerable, so the verse cannot justify cruelty, abandonment, or cultic isolation.

questions.question: Why compare discipleship to a tower and a war council?
questions.answer: Both builders and kings must assess whether they can finish; public failure and defeat are at stake. Jesus turns crowds' enthusiasm into sober consent to the road's cost. The comparisons do not mean disciples possess sufficient resources alone — the outmatched king especially learns surrender — but they exclude impulsive self-deception.

questions.question: Can salt really lose saltiness?
questions.answer: The text does not explain how; it says only that such salt is fit ‘neither for the soil nor for the manure pile.’ The image warns that a disciple who abandons the distinctive allegiance just described cannot fulfill the role represented by salt. It is a durability warning, not chemistry instruction.

glossary.def: Visible swelling caused by fluid retention, which can indicate an underlying illness.
Social system of gifts and return obligation; here, guests who ‘might also return the favor, and pay you back’ (14:12).
Acceptance of shame, loss, and possible death on Jesus's road, not generic inconvenience.
Say farewell to or relinquish claim over; Luke applies it to all possessions.
